full_judgment: 33. It was also submitted that the ICT-1 erred in law by failing to direct itself as to the law of judicial notice and also to the fact that the purpose of the law of judicial notice is to promote fair trial and, as such, acted unlawfully in failing to notify the defence of the proposal to take judicial notice of certain facts and failing to hear legal submissions on the issue. It was submitted that ICT-1 erred in law by purporting to take judicial notice of contentious issues and also by relying on sources which were not in evidence, and which the defence had no notice of. It was submitted that the ICT-1 further erred in law by failing to respect the fundamental principle of nullum crimen sine lege and the consequent right of the appellant to know the case against him, including a legal characterisation of the facts to accord both with the crimes and the precise form of participation by failing to distinguish clearly between direct perpetration and complicity, and also by not charging with superior responsibility although a verdict of guilt was passed. It was submitted that ICT-1 erred in law by failing to define 'participation' under section 3(2) to reflect customary international law in 1971 and hence failed in its application of the law of 'participation' to the charges framed against the convict appellant. It was submitted that ICT-1 erred in law and in fact by failing to apply the appropriate burden and standard of proof to the charges faced by the appellant. It was submitted that attribute disproportionate weight to the testimony of prosecution witnesses vis-a-vis the defence witnesses, and prosecution documentary evidence vis-à-vis the defence documentary evidence in its findings with respect to the appellant and, as such, the conviction.
